title: PowerShell tutorial: cmdlets, pipeline, variables and scripts — cv.cm
description: Learn PowerShell scripting step by step: run a .ps1 script, cmdlets and the object pipeline, variables, operators, functions, hashtables and try/catch errors.
answer: PowerShell is Microsoft's cross-platform shell and scripting language for automation. Its commands, called cmdlets, pass .NET objects through the pipeline instead of plain text, so you can filter, sort and export data without parsing. This page covers installing PowerShell 7, running scripts, cmdlets, variables, operators, control flow, functions, collections and error handling.

sections.h: What PowerShell is and what it is used for
body: PowerShell is a cross-platform shell and scripting language from Microsoft, built on .NET. Unlike traditional shells, which pass plain text between commands, PowerShell passes .NET objects with properties and methods, so you can filter and sort data without parsing text.

System administrators and DevOps engineers use PowerShell to automate Windows, manage Active Directory, Microsoft 365 and Azure, and write build and deployment scripts. There are two editions: Windows PowerShell 5.1, which is built into Windows, and PowerShell 7 and later (command name `pwsh`), which is open source and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. This tutorial targets PowerShell 7.

sections.h: Install PowerShell and run Hello, world
body: On Windows, install PowerShell 7 with `winget install --id Microsoft.PowerShell --source winget`; on macOS and Linux, use Homebrew or the package manager described in Microsoft's install guide. Scripts are text files with the `.ps1` extension.

On Windows, the execution policy may block scripts. `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned` allows your own local scripts while still requiring downloaded scripts to be signed. Visual Studio Code with the PowerShell extension is the recommended editor.

Commands are called cmdlets and follow a `Verb-Noun` naming pattern, such as `Get-Process`, `Set-Location` or `New-Item`. Three cmdlets help you explore everything else: `Get-Command`, `Get-Help` and `Get-Member`.

body.code:
Get-Command -Noun Process          # list commands that work with processes
Get-Help Get-ChildItem -Examples   # show usage examples

# five processes using the most memory
Get-Process |
    Sort-Object -Property WorkingSet64 -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 5 -Property Name, Id, WorkingSet64

# files larger than 1 MB in the current folder
Get-ChildItem -File | Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB } |
    ForEach-Object { "{0}  {1:N0} KB" -f $_.Name, ($_.Length / 1KB) }

Get-Date | Get-Member -MemberType Property   # inspect an object

body: Inside a script block, `$_` (or `$PSItem`) is the current object in the pipeline. Because objects keep their types, `Sort-Object` sorts numbers numerically and dates chronologically without extra work.

Variables start with `$`. They hold any .NET object, and you can add a type constraint in square brackets. Double-quoted strings expand variables and `$( )` expressions; single-quoted strings are literal.

body.code:
$name = "Ada"
[int]$count = 3
$price = 19.99                      # System.Double
$isAdmin = $false
$today = Get-Date

"Hello, $name"                      # Hello, Ada
"Next: $($count + 1)"               # Next: 4
'No $expansion here'                # No $expansion here
$price.GetType().Name               # Double
$today.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd")       # for example 2026-10-31
[int]"42" + 1                       # 43 (explicit conversion)

body: Comparison operators are words, not symbols: `-eq`, `-ne`, `-gt`, `-lt`, `-ge`, `-le`, `-like` (wildcards), `-match` (regular expressions) and `-contains`. String comparisons are case-insensitive unless you use the `c` versions such as `-ceq`.

body.note: Using `>` or `=` to compare is the classic mistake: `if ($a > 5)` redirects `$a` to a file named `5`, and `=` assigns. Use `-gt` and `-eq`. When comparing with `$null`, put `$null` on the left (`$null -eq $x`) so that arrays are not filtered by accident.

body: Functions use `param()` blocks to declare typed, named parameters. Adding `[CmdletBinding()]` gives a function the same common parameters as built-in cmdlets, such as `-Verbose`. Any output that is not captured becomes the function's return value.

body.code:
function Get-Greeting {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)]
        [string]$Name,
        [string]$Greeting = "Hello"
    )
    Write-Verbose "Building greeting for $Name"
    "$Greeting, $Name!"
}

Get-Greeting -Name "Ann"                  # Hello, Ann!
Get-Greeting -Name "Bo" -Greeting "Hi"    # Hi, Bo!
Get-Greeting "Cy" -Verbose                # also prints the verbose message

body: Call functions like cmdlets, with spaces between arguments: `Get-Greeting -Name Ann`. Writing `Get-Greeting("Ann", "Hi")` passes a single array argument, a frequent surprise for people coming from other languages.

Arrays are created with `@( )` or a comma-separated list. Hashtables, written `@{ }`, store key-value pairs. `[pscustomobject]` turns a hashtable into an object that works well with `Sort-Object`, `Format-Table` and `Export-Csv`.

body.code:
$langs = @("PowerShell", "Python")
$langs += "Go"                       # creates a new, longer array
$langs.Count                         # 3
$langs[0]                            # PowerShell
$langs -contains "Go"                # True

$ports = @{ http = 80; https = 443 }
$ports["ssh"] = 22
$ports.https                         # 443
$ports.Keys.Count                    # 3

$user = [pscustomobject]@{ Name = "Ann"; Age = 31 }
$user.Name                           # Ann
$people = @(
    [pscustomobject]@{ Name = "Bo"; Age = 25 }
    $user
)
$people | Sort-Object Age | Format-Table

body: Adding to an array with `+=` copies the whole array each time. For large loops, collect the loop output directly (`$result = foreach (...) { ... }`) or use a `[System.Collections.Generic.List[object]]`.

PowerShell has terminating errors, which stop execution, and non-terminating errors, which print a message and continue. `try`/`catch`/`finally` only catches terminating errors, so add `-ErrorAction Stop` to a cmdlet when you want to catch its failures.
Inside `catch`, `$_` is the error record. Setting `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` at the top of a script is a common way to fail fast.

sections.h: A small complete script: disk usage report
body: This script lists the largest files under a folder, groups them by extension and exports a CSV report. It combines parameters, the pipeline, calculated properties and error handling.

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: using `>`, `<` or `==` instead of `-gt`, `-lt` and `-eq`; calling functions with parentheses and commas; forgetting `-ErrorAction Stop` inside `try`; using `Write-Host` for data (it writes to the screen, not the pipeline, so prefer `Write-Output` or plain values); and mixing up Windows PowerShell 5.1 with PowerShell 7.

ul: PowerShell 101 and the PowerShell documentation on Microsoft Learn.
`Get-Help about_*` in the shell, for example `Get-Help about_Operators`; run `Update-Help` first.
The PowerShell Gallery, the official repository of modules, used with `Install-Module`.
PSScriptAnalyzer, a linter that checks scripts against recommended practices.

faq.q: What is the difference between PowerShell and Windows PowerShell?
faq.a: Windows PowerShell 5.1 is the older edition built into Windows and based on .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 and later is the cross-platform, open-source edition based on modern .NET, started with the `pwsh` command.

faq.q: Is PowerShell the same as Command Prompt?
faq.a: No. Command Prompt (`cmd.exe`) runs batch commands and passes text. PowerShell is a full scripting language that passes objects, although it can still run most command-line programs.

faq.q: Can PowerShell run on Linux and macOS?
faq.a: Yes. PowerShell 7 and later runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, although some Windows-specific modules are only available on Windows.

faq.q: Why can't I run my .ps1 script?
faq.a: The execution policy on Windows may block it. Run `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`, and start scripts with a path, such as `./script.ps1`.
`$_` (also `$PSItem`) is the current object in the pipeline, used inside script blocks for cmdlets such as `Where-Object` and `ForEach-Object`, and the current error inside `catch`.
